core: Verbs as action, occurrence, and state words
Linking verbs (be, seem, become) and their subject-connecting work
Transitive and intransitive verbs and the direct object
Main verbs, auxiliary (helping) verbs, and modal auxiliaries
Main verb forms: base, third-person -s, -ing, past, past participle
Choosing precise verbs when revising writing

claims.claim: A verb expresses an action (physical or mental), an occurrence, or a state of being, and a clause cannot stand as a sentence without one.
Linking verbs such as be, seem, and become connect the subject to a word or phrase that renames or describes it, and some verbs can act as either action or linking verbs depending on the sentence.

A direct object is the word or phrase on the receiving end of the verb, answering what or whom; a transitive verb takes a direct object while an intransitive verb does not, and many verbs can be used either way.

Auxiliary (helping) verbs, commonly forms of be, have, and do plus the modal auxiliaries can, could, may, might, must, shall, should, will, and would, combine with a main verb to form a verb phrase and add meanings of time, ability, possibility, permission, or obligation.
Modal auxiliaries are followed by the base form of the main verb and do not change to agree with the subject.

English verbs have principal forms, base, third-person -s, -ing (present participle), past, and past participle, that serve as building blocks for verb phrases; regular verbs form the past and past participle with -ed, while irregular verbs vary and participles appear after helping verbs.
A phrasal verb combines a main verb with a particle such as off, up, or out, and the combination can carry a meaning different from the verb alone.
Precise, specific verbs strengthen writing, while sentences that lean on be and other general words can be revised to carry more information per word.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How verb categories are named and divided across grammars.
positions: Business Grammar organizes verbs into action, linking, and helping types.
Writing for Success and Purdue OWL describe linking verbs, helping verbs, and sentence patterns with somewhat different terms.
Some grammar traditions use 'copular verb' or 'state verb' instead of 'linking verb.'
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses the common action/linking/helping division, notes that helping verbs are also called auxiliary verbs, and keeps terminology consistent while acknowledging that naming conventions vary across frameworks.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether verbs like look, smell, and taste are linking or action verbs.
positions: Business Grammar treats sensing verbs as a type of linking verb when they describe the subject (e.g., 'It tastes delicious').
The same words act as action verbs when the subject performs the sensing (e.g., 'Marta looked at the receipt').
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the context test: if the word connects the subject to a description, it is linking; if it names something the subject does, it is action. Original examples avoid reproducing source sentences.

unsupportedExistingClaims: No prior machine-generated draft existed for this topic in public/content/phase-3/lessons.json, so there were no draft claims to verify or discard; the lesson was written directly from sources.
correctionsNeeded: Built the lesson from source-verified accounts of verb types, objects, auxiliaries, forms, and phrasal verbs rather than from template text.
Named the five main verb forms without teaching tense usage, explicitly deferring tenses and subject-verb agreement to their sibling topics.
Added original example sentences throughout and a five-question bank with a spread answer key (A, C, B, D, A) including recall and application/analysis items.

sourceRecords.title: 2.4 Verbs — Business Grammar
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B. Read live on 2026-08-21 (URL 2-5-verbs redirects to 2-4-verbs; canonical slug used). Supports: a verb shows actions, occurrences, or a state of being; no sentence without a verb; main (action) verbs; linking verbs (is, am, are, was, seem, became) likened to an equals sign; helping verbs forming verb phrases with an action verb; modal verbs showing ability, possibility, obligation, permission, or condition. Reference only; examples in the lesson are original.

sourceRecords.title: 7.1 Types of Verbs — Business Grammar
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B. Read live on 2026-08-21. Supports: action verbs describe something happening; linking verbs rename or describe the subject and include forms of to be plus sensing verbs; helping verbs (also called auxiliary verbs) combine with an action verb to create a verb phrase and add time, ability, possibility, or request; the helper list including be, can, could, do, have, might, must, shall, should, will, would. Reference only; no wording adapted.

sourceRecords.title: 7.3 Verb Participles — Business Grammar

Reference only.
